# Have you gone through Topics 6 and 7 from the Week 3 content yet? 

## You might be thinking...

> Okay, but why Quarto? Why should we use another tool to code in R? 

## Why Quarto? {.smaller}

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="70%"}
Combine your **code**, its **results**, and your **prose** into fully reproducible documents 

* **unified ecosystem** allows you to create documents, books, websites, blogs, and presentations natively without any extension packages to additional tools 
* **multi-language support** and **consistent syntax** across all supported programming languages (code written in the code blocks is what varies)

:::

::: {.column width="30%"}
![](images/logo-quarto.png)
:::

::::: 


## {#slide11-id data-menu-title="Why authoring tool"}

A Quarto workflow is...

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
#### Less

* Error-prone
* Time consuming (once you get the hang of it)

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
#### More 

* Dynamic 
* Reproducible
* Transparent 

:::
:::::

![Artwork by Alison Horst](images/quarto-illustration-detail.png)

## {#slide12-id data-menu-title="Why authoring tool continued"}

The dynamic document holds code & narrative surrounding the data -- **an authoring framework for data science!**

* Can be used to…
  - Reproduce your analyses 
  - Collaborate and share code with others 
  - Communicate your findings with others (even those who do not understand code)

## {#slide13-id data-menu-title="Why authoring tool continued still" transition="none"}

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="75%"}

* Present analyses in **high quality** documents, reports, and presentations 
* Support **dozens of output formats**, like HTMLs, PDFs, Word files, slideshows, and more
* Documents are **fully reproducible** — you can update your document at any time by re-rendering the code blocks
* Can use **multiple programming languages** including R, Python, and SQL

:::

:::{.column width="25%"}

![](images/logo-quarto.png){.absolute top=150}

:::
:::::

::::: {.columns}

1. Literate Programming

4. A templating tool

# Ingredients in a Quarto recipe

## (1) YAML = metadata 

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

* Save output options here 
* Different syntax/language than the rest of the document - `key: value` pair syntax  
* Watch out for your spaces!

:::

:::{.column width="45%"}

![](images/YAML_ex1.png)

![](images/YAML_ex2.png)

:::
:::::

## (2) Text and (3) Code 

* Text written following *Markdown*

* Code blocks! 
  - You can think of each block sort of like a mini-script file within the larger document

![](images/together_at_last.png){fig-align="center"}

## Markdown overview

> A Markdown-formatted document should be publishable as-is, as plain text, without looking like it’s been marked up with tags or formatting instructions. – [John Gruber](https://daringfireball.net/projects/markdown/syntax#philosophy)

See [Quarto Website](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html) for more details/a reference on the markdown flavor used in Quarto (i.e., pandoc)

## Code blocks

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
* 3 backticks to open and 3 to close to the code block
* `{r}` specifies the language 

::: 

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/codeblock-R.png)
:::
:::::

## Code block options 

* Specified in a special comment at the top of the block (`#|` called a "hashpipe")
* Specify multiple options with multiple `#|` lines
* Also follow YAML with `key: value` pairs 

## Code block options  {transition="none"}

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
You can set **global block options** (default of how all code block behave) in the YAML with `execute`

* You can (and should) use individual block options too 

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/execute_YAML.png)

:::
:::::

## Code block options {transition="none" .smaller}

| option       	| default 	| effect                                               	|
|--------------	|---------	|------------------------------------------------------	|
| `eval`       	| `true`  	| Whether to evaluate the code and include its results 	|
| `echo`       	| `true`  	| Whether to display code along with its results       	|
| `warning`    	| `true`  	| Whether to display warnings                          	|
| `message`    	| `true`  	| Whether to display messages                          	|
| `fig-width`  	| 7       	| Width in inches for plots created in the code block  	|
| `fig-height` 	| 5       	| Height in inches for plots created in the code block 	| 

[Reference page with the full list of options](https://quarto.org/docs/reference/cells/cells-knitr.html)

## Block labels 

| Good     	| Bad            	|
|----------	|----------------	|
| my-plot  	| my_plot        	|
| myplot   	| my plot        	|
| myplot1  	| anything else! 	|
| myplot-1 	|                	|
| MY-PLOT  	|                	|

* *No duplicate* block labels! You will get an error
* Automatic cross-reference code blocks that produce a figure or table with `fig-name` or `tbl-name`

# Let's practice! 

## Pair Programming 

* Structured group work 
* 2 roles: **Driver** and **Navigator** 
  1. **Driver** = active person typing, problem-solving, thinking out loud
  2. **Navigator** = reflective person, looks out for bugs, offers advice 
  
![](images/C12_pair-programming-overview_keyboard_switch.png){fig-align="center"}
